lesson.text: The road is hostile. The message must not be helpless.

Secure communication rests on four guarantees — you enforced all four yourself, on the Post Road and in the forged-letter affair. Name them plainly now, because every real protocol you meet afterward is some arrangement of these four.

THE FOUR GUARANTEES

AUTHENTICATION — proof the sender is who they claim. (The seal ring only its holder can press.)

INTEGRITY — proof the message arrived unchanged. (The wax seal across the fold, broken if opened.)

CONFIDENTIALITY — only the intended reader can read it. (The locked box on the hostile road.)

NON-REPUDIATION — the sender cannot later deny sending it. (One's own seal, undeniable.)

Two of these look alike but point opposite ways. AUTHENTICATION protects you FROM impostors pretending to be the sender. NON-REPUDIATION protects the RECIPIENT from a real sender who later denies their own message. Same unforgeable-identity property; opposite direction of defence.

THE SEAL vs THE WATCHWORD

A shared WATCHWORD — a secret both sides know — is weak proof of identity: anyone who ever learned it can use it, and you cannot tell who did. A SEAL bound to one person — something only they can produce — is strong, because producing it requires something they alone hold. This is the leap from a shared password to a cryptographic identity: the single most important upgrade in the history of secure messaging.
Which raises the real question of authentication: how do we bind proof to a PERSON? There are three kinds of evidence, called the three FACTORS.

THE THREE FACTORS OF AUTHENTICATION

SOMETHING YOU KNOW — a password, a watchword, a secret phrase. Weakest alone: it can be told, guessed, or stolen without you ever noticing.

SOMETHING YOU HAVE — a seal ring, a key, a physical token. Stronger: stealing it usually means you NOTICE it's gone.

SOMETHING YOU ARE — a face, a voice, a fingerprint (biometrics). Hard to copy, impossible to forget — but impossible to change if it's ever compromised.

Combine two or more from DIFFERENT categories and you have MULTI-FACTOR authentication: a stolen watchword is useless without the ring; a stolen ring is useless without the face. The forged Council letter failed precisely because it carried only the watchword — one factor, and the weakest one.

One caution the village already learned the hard way, back at Maren's ledger: the "something you are" factor is BIOMETRIC, which is special-category personal data. Strong authentication and heavy data-protection duty arrive together — the more powerful the proof of identity, the more sensitive the thing you must now protect.
These guarantees are not a menu to pick from. A serious channel wants all four, layered, on the assumption that the road is always hostile. Assume breach; build anyway.

quiz.q: A letter arrives bearing a watchword known to the whole Council. What does the watchword actually prove?
choices: That the sender is a Council member
explain: A watchword can't prove membership — it only proves someone knows the word, Council member or not.
Exactly — a shared secret proves knowledge of the secret, not identity. Anyone who acquired it — a bribed clerk, a leak — passes. Authentication needs something unforgeable, not just something known.
That's integrity's job. A watchword says nothing about whether the contents were changed in transit.

quiz.q: You crack open a letter and find the wax seal spanning its fold broken and re-pressed. Which guarantee is now in doubt?
explain: Confidentiality is about who can READ the message — a broken seal doesn't tell you that.

Exactly — the tamper-seal binds to the sealed contents; a broken seal means the message may have been altered in transit. Confidentiality is about who can read it; integrity is about whether it changed.
Non-repudiation is about the sender denying the message later — a broken seal is a road-tampering problem, not a denial problem.

quiz.q: The Council sends Bram a sensitive reply across bandit country. They lock the contents in a sealed box but leave the destination address on the outside, plainly readable. Why leave the address plain?
choices: Laziness — nobody got around to hiding it
So couriers can route it — purpose limitation in practice
explain: Not laziness — it's deliberate. Leaving anything unnecessary exposed would BE the failure here.

Exactly — the courier needs the routing data and nothing more; sealing the contents protects the secret while the plain address keeps the system working. Seal what must be hidden, not what must be used to make the system function.
Addresses can absolutely be sealed too — the choice to leave this one plain is deliberate, not a technical limit.

quiz.q: A signature only its owner can produce, that they cannot later disown, provides —
explain: Confidentiality is about who can read the message — it says nothing about who sent it or whether they can later deny it.
Exactly — an identity-bound mark only the sender can produce, which they can't later disown. It protects the recipient FROM the sender, where authentication protects the recipient FROM impostors.
Integrity is about whether the message changed in transit, not about the sender disowning it afterward.

quiz.q: The gate guard admits only someone who speaks the watchword AND presents their seal ring AND is recognized by face. Which authentication factors are in play?
explain: Not quite — the seal ring and the face aren't things you KNOW, they're things you HAVE and something you ARE.

Exactly — watchword = something you KNOW, seal ring = something you HAVE, face = something you ARE: three different factors, the strongest posture, because compromising one doesn't compromise the others. Note that the "something you are" check (the face) is biometric — special-category data that must itself be protected.
The watchword and the face aren't 'something you have' — this gate genuinely combines three different factor types.
